chapter_summary:
Optimizing CloudFront performance and security goes beyond basic distribution setup; it involves leveraging advanced features to fine-tune caching, protect against threats, and customize delivery logic. For performance, the primary goal is to maximize cache hit ratios and minimize the load on your origin servers. This starts with effective **cache policies**. Beyond simply setting a TTL, you must carefully consider which headers, query strings, and cookies are essential for your content's uniqueness and personalization. Forwarding too many can lead to a low cache hit ratio, as CloudFront treats each unique combination as a separate object. Conversely, not forwarding enough can result in incorrect or stale content being served. CloudFront offers managed cache policies (e.g., `CachingOptimized`, `Managed-CachingDisabled`) and allows creating custom policies for granular control.

Another critical performance feature is **compression at the edge**. CloudFront can automatically compress files (e.g., Gzip, Brotli) before delivering them to viewers, reducing the amount of data transferred and speeding up page load times. This offloads compression from your origin server. For complex architectures, especially those with multiple CDNs or a high volume of requests to a single origin, **CloudFront Origin Shield** can significantly reduce origin load. Origin Shield acts as an intermediate caching layer between your CloudFront Edge Locations and your origin. All requests that result in a cache miss at an Edge Location are routed through Origin Shield first. This means if multiple Edge Locations request the same content from the origin, only Origin Shield makes the request, effectively consolidating requests and improving cache hit ratios at the origin level.

**Lambda@Edge** is a powerful tool for customizing content delivery. It allows you to run Node.js or Python code at CloudFront Edge Locations in response to four types of events: viewer request, viewer response, origin request, and origin response. This enables dynamic modifications to requests or responses without hitting your origin. For example, you can use Lambda@Edge to:
*   Rewrite URLs for SEO or routing purposes.
*   Perform A/B testing by routing users to different origins based on headers or cookies.
*   Add security headers (e.g., HSTS, CSP) to responses.
*   Implement custom authentication or authorization logic.
*   Inject dynamic content or personalize responses.
*   Normalize query strings or headers to improve cache hit ratios.

However, Lambda@Edge has execution limits (e.g., memory, duration), so it's best suited for lightweight, latency-sensitive logic.

On the security front, CloudFront integrates seamlessly with **AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall)**. By associating a WAF Web ACL with your CloudFront distribution, you can protect your application from common web exploits and bots that might affect availability, compromise security, or consume excessive resources. WAF rules can block malicious IP addresses, filter specific HTTP request attributes, and mitigate DDoS attacks at the application layer. For private content, **signed URLs and signed cookies** are essential. These mechanisms allow you to grant temporary, time-limited access to specific content in your CloudFront distribution, ensuring only authorized users can view premium or restricted files. Signed URLs are typically used for individual files, while signed cookies are better for granting access to multiple files within a directory or for an entire session.

Another advanced security feature is **field-level encryption**. This allows you to encrypt specific data fields in HTTP requests at the CloudFront Edge Location before the requests are forwarded to your origin. This ensures that sensitive data (e.g., personally identifiable information, credit card numbers) remains encrypted throughout the entire application stack, even if your origin server is compromised, only the application with the private key can decrypt it. This provides an additional layer of data protection beyond HTTPS.

Finally, managing **cache invalidation** is crucial for ensuring content freshness. While setting appropriate TTLs is the first step, sometimes you need to remove content from the cache immediately (e.g., after an urgent update or a security patch). CloudFront allows you to invalidate specific paths (e.g., `/index.html`, `/images/*`) or even `/*` (all content). However, invalidations should be used judiciously as they can incur costs and temporarily increase origin load. A common mistake is to invalidate `/*` too frequently, negating the benefits of caching. Instead, consider versioning your assets (e.g., `main.css?v=2`) or using unique file names to avoid invalidation altogether for frequently updated content. Always monitor your CloudFront metrics (cache hit ratio, error rates, origin latency) to identify areas for optimization and ensure your distribution is performing as expected.

screens.title: Optimizing CloudFront Performance and Security
screens.subtitle: Advanced caching, edge customization, and distribution hardening

narration.text: In this chapter we will explore the collection of features that make CloudFront both fast and secure. You will learn how cache policies, compression at the edge, and Origin Shield work together to reduce origin load and improve cache hit ratios. We will also cover how Lambda@Edge lets you run short, latency-sensitive logic at the edge to rewrite requests, add security headers, or personalize content without routing traffic back to your origin. On the security side, you will see how AWS WAF, signed URLs and cookies, and field-level encryption protect both availability and sensitive data. I will walk you through concrete examples: creating a cache policy that avoids forwarding unnecessary headers, deploying a small Lambda@Edge to add strict security headers, and choosing when to use Origin Shield to consolidate origin requests. Finally, you will gain strategies for managing cache invalidation and asset versioning so updates are safe and predictable. By the end of this lesson you should be able to apply these features to both reduce cost and improve security, and know common mistakes to avoid when tuning CloudFront.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Effective cache control and edge customization both cut origin load and improve user experience, while security features protect integrity and data privacy at scale.

screens.title: Cache Policies and Cache Hit Ratio
screens.subtitle: How what you forward determines cache effectiveness

narration.text: A cache policy defines how CloudFront treats incoming requests for caching. It specifies which headers, cookies, and query strings are forwarded to the origin and the TTL behavior. The core trade-off is simple: forwarding more request attributes increases content correctness and personalization but reduces cache hit ratio because CloudFront treats each unique combination as a separate cache key. Conversely, forwarding too little risks serving stale or incorrect content. A concrete example: if you forward a personalization header for a storefront user name, each unique header value creates a new cached object and dramatically lowers hits for static resources. Instead, forward only the authentication cookie when needed and keep public assets generic. Use managed cache policies like CachingOptimized when you want a sensible default for static assets, and create custom policies for APIs or dynamic pages where query strings matter. Also consider normalizing headers or query strings with Lambda@Edge to canonicalize requests and increase hits. A common misconception is that longer TTLs always improve performance; they do reduce origin calls but can increase the chance of stale content. The takeaway: design cache keys deliberately—forward the minimum attributes required for correctness and use versioning for frequent updates.

keyIdea.title: Cache policy takeaway
keyIdea.text: Forward only necessary request attributes and use asset versioning to keep caches both efficient and fresh.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Cache Policies
Definition
What a cache policy controls
  • Which headers, cookies, and query strings are forwarded.
  • Default, minimum and maximum TTLs for cached objects.
  • Whether requests are cacheable based on method and authorization.
Example
E-commerce static assets should use CachingOptimized. For user-specific pages, forward an authentication cookie only when necessary, and keep product images cacheable without personalization.
Key Takeaway
Minimize forwarded attributes for public assets; version files for updates instead of frequent invalidation.
How to improve hit ratio
Normalize Requests
Use Lambda@Edge to canonicalize headers or remove tracking query strings that do not affect content identity.
Versioning
Use unique file names or query parameters for new releases to avoid invalidations.
Common mistake
Forwarding many headers to preserve personalization by default, which reduces cache hits. Instead, forward only what is essential and use edge logic for minor variations.

screens.title: Compression at the Edge
screens.subtitle: Reducing transfer size without touching the origin

narration.text: Compression at the edge has a straightforward goal: reduce the number of bytes delivered to viewers by letting CloudFront compress responses with Gzip or Brotli before sending them. This offloads C P U work from your origin and speeds page loads for users, especially on slower networks. A practical approach is to let CloudFront compress text-based assets if your origin serves them uncompressed. If the origin already serves pre-compressed versions with the correct content-encoding header, CloudFront should be configured to forward those as-is. Consider when automatic edge compression is not ideal: very small files, already compressed binary formats, or when you have pre-compressed multiple variants and want full control. To decide, measure bandwidth and C P U at the origin before and after enabling compression. A common misconception is that enabling edge compression always reduces latency. In some cases, added C P U work at the edge can add microseconds; the net gain is usually positive for larger text assets but negligible for tiny files. The takeaway: enable edge compression for text-heavy responses, prefer pre-compression when you must control binary variants, and validate with metrics.

keyIdea.title: Edge compression tip
keyIdea.text: Compress at the edge for large text assets; use pre-compression when you manage multiple content encodings.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Edge Compression
Process
How edge compression works
Origin responses
Origin returns content. If uncompressed, CloudFront can compress before delivery.
Edge compression
CloudFront applies Gzip or Brotli based on viewer Accept-Encoding and serves the compressed payload.
Viewer delivery
Viewer receives a smaller response and renders faster, reducing bandwidth costs.
Example
A site serving large CSS and JavaScript files gains reduced page load time when CloudFront compresses these files at the edge rather than relying on the origin CPU.
Common misconception
Some assume compression always lowers latency. For very small files or already compressed types, savings are negligible and can add overhead.
Key Takeaway

Edge compression reduces transfer size for text assets and offloads origin CPU; verify impact with metrics before broad rollout.

screens.title: CloudFront Origin Shield
screens.subtitle: An intermediate caching layer to protect your origin

narration.text: Origin Shield is an additional caching layer positioned between CloudFront edge locations and your origin that consolidates cache-miss traffic. When an edge location does not have an object, it queries Origin Shield instead of the origin directly. If multiple edge locations request the same object, only Origin Shield fetches it from the origin, which reduces burst load and request volume at your origin. This is particularly valuable in architectures with many edge locations or when using multiple CDNs that may funnel requests to the same origin. A concrete scenario: a global release of a new asset can generate simultaneous cache misses across regions; enabling Origin Shield ensures one consolidated request to your origin rather than many, smoothing origin load and improving overall cache performance. Origin Shield does not change cache key semantics; it is best combined with careful cache policies and request normalization to maximize consolidated hits. A common misconception is to rely solely on longer TTLs for origin protection; Origin Shield adds resilience during sudden spikes and when TTLs are intentionally short. The takeaway: enable Origin Shield strategically to reduce origin request volume and improve resilience under load.

keyIdea.title: Origin Shield insight
keyIdea.text: Use Origin Shield to consolidate cache misses and protect origin capacity during global traffic spikes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Origin Shield
Role
Centralized intermediate cache
When an edge location misses, it asks Origin Shield. Origin Shield will fetch from the origin only once for a given object, reducing duplicate origin calls across edges.
Benefit
Fewer origin requests and improved origin stability under global load.
When to use
High global traffic, multi-CDN edges, or frequent simultaneous misses during releases.
Example scenario
During a worldwide product launch, edge locations generate cache misses for a new asset. With Origin Shield enabled, only Origin Shield fetches once from the origin and distributes to edges, protecting the origin from a surge of duplicate requests.
Common mistake
Assuming Origin Shield is a substitute for well-designed cache keys. It helps on misses but does not replace the need to reduce unnecessary cache fragmentation.

screens.title: Lambda@Edge: Add Security Headers
screens.subtitle: Deploy a lightweight function to harden responses

narration.text: Lambda@Edge runs small functions at CloudFront edge locations in response to viewer or origin events. It is ideal for low-latency tasks such as adding security headers, URL rewrites, or simple routing decisions. The provided example adds common security headers on viewer response events, including Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, and Content-Security-Policy. Deploying such a function reduces risk by ensuring headers are present for every response at the edge, without modifying origin code. Keep in mind Lambda@Edge functions have execution and memory limits, so they must be compact and fast. A common mistake is to implement heavy logic or long-running tasks at the edge; that will fail or increase latency. In practice you create the function in us-east-1, attach a minimal IAM role that includes basic execution permissions, add edgelambda. amazonaws. com to the trust policy, then deploy to your distribution as a Viewer Response trigger. After deployment, validate using browser developer tools and inspect the response headers to confirm the function added the security directives. The takeaway: Lambda@Edge is a powerful place to apply consistent, low-latency security headers across your distribution but keep functions small and idempotent.

keyIdea.title: Lambda@Edge caution
keyIdea.text: Use for fast, idempotent modifications only; avoid complex or long-running operations at the edge.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Lambda@Edge Code
Purpose
Add security headers on viewer response
This function demonstrates adding HSTS, X-Frame-Options, and other headers at the edge so every viewer response carries consistent security policies.
Notes
  • Create function in us-east-1 and deploy to Viewer Response.
  • Attach minimal execution role and add edgelambda.amazonaws.com to trust policy.
  • Keep logic small to stay within execution limits.
Code example
'use strict';
exports.handler = (event, context, callback) => {
  const response = event.Records[0].cf.response;
  const headers = response.headers;

  // Add security headers
  headers['strict-transport-security'] = [{ key: 'Strict-Transport-Security', value: 'max-age=63072000; includeSubdomains; preload' }];
  headers['x-content-type-options'] = [{ key: 'X-Content-Type-Options', value: 'nosniff' }];
  headers['x-frame-options'] = [{ key: 'X-Frame-Options', value: 'DENY' }];
  headers['x-xss-protection'] = [{ key: 'X-XSS-Protection', value: '1; mode=block' }];
  headers['referrer-policy'] = [{ key: 'Referrer-Policy', value: 'no-referrer-when-downgrade' }];
  headers['content-security-policy'] = [{ key: 'Content-Security-Policy', value: "default-src 'self' *.cloudfront.net;" }]; // Customize as needed

  callback(null, response);
};
Validation
After deployment, inspect response headers in browser developer tools to confirm the security headers appear on viewer responses.

screens.title: AWS WAF Integration
screens.subtitle: Protect at the edge with Web ACLs and managed rules

narration.text: AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) provides rule-based protection for web applications and integrates directly with CloudFront distributions. By associating a Web ACL with a distribution, you filter malicious traffic at the edge before it reaches your origin. WAF rules can block or allow based on IP addresses, headers, URI strings, or request body patterns, and managed rule groups offer protection against common threats like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting. A practical deployment pattern is to attach a Web ACL as part of your distribution deployment pipeline, start with managed rule groups to provide baseline protection, and then add custom rules for application-specific patterns or known malicious IP sets. WAF is not a substitute for secure coding or network-level protections, but it reduces attack surface at the application layer. A typical misconception is that WAF alone eliminates the need for monitoring; in reality you should combine WAF with logging and metrics to tune rules and avoid false positives. The takeaway: integrate WAF to stop common web exploits at the edge, and iterate rules with monitoring to balance protection and availability.

keyIdea.title: WAF summary
keyIdea.text: Use WAF to filter application-layer attacks at the edge and refine rules using logs and metrics to avoid blocking legitimate traffic.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › AWS WAF
What it does
Application-layer filtering at the edge
WAF inspects HTTP requests and applies rules to block or allow traffic, protecting against attacks like SQL injection and XSS and enabling IP filtering.
Deployment notes
  • Associate a Web ACL with your CloudFront distribution.
  • Start with managed rules then add custom rules for application needs.
  • Use logging and metrics to refine rules and reduce false positives.
Example
Attach a Web ACL that blocks common exploit patterns and add an IP set rule to block known bad actors identified by your security team.
Common mistake
Overly broad rules that block legitimate traffic. Use logs and staged deployments to tune rules safely.
Key Takeaway

WAF applied at CloudFront stops threats before they reach your origin, but must be tuned with logs to avoid availability issues.

screens.title: Signed URLs vs Signed Cookies & Field-Level Encryption
screens.subtitle: Access control and protecting sensitive fields

narration.text: When distributing private content, CloudFront offers signed URLs and signed cookies to enforce time-limited access. Signed URLs are best for granting access to an individual file, where you generate a cryptographic signature tied to a resource and an expiration. Signed cookies are more suitable when you need to grant access across multiple files or an entire directory for a session, without signing every URL individually. A common misconception is using signed URLs for session-like access; signed cookies are simpler in that scenario. Field-level encryption addresses a different problem: protecting sensitive request data in transit and at the origin. With field-level encryption, certain HTTP request fields are encrypted at the CloudFront edge, so they remain encrypted until decrypted by the application that holds the private key. This protects PII or payment data even if the origin stack is partially compromised. An example approach is to use signed cookies for media streaming session access and field-level encryption to protect submitted credit card fields on checkout forms. The takeaway: choose signed URLs for per-file control, signed cookies for session-level access, and employ field-level encryption for targeted data protection.

keyIdea.title: Access and data protection
keyIdea.text: Use the right tool: signed URLs for single assets, signed cookies for sessions, and field-level encryption for sensitive fields.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Signed Access & Encryption
Signed URLs
Best for single-file access. Signature tied to a resource and expiry, commonly used for downloads or protected assets.
Signed Cookies
Best for session-level access across many files. Easier when granting temporary access to directories or streaming sessions.
Field-Level Encryption
Encrypt specific HTTP request fields at the edge so only the origin application can decrypt them with the private key.
Concrete scenario
Use signed cookies to grant a logged-in user access to a set of media files for their session and use field-level encryption for payment fields submitted during checkout so sensitive data remains encrypted until processed by the origin application.
Key Takeaway

Pick signed URLs for single items, signed cookies for sessions, and field-level encryption to protect sensitive fields in transit to the origin.

screens.title: Cache Invalidation and Asset Versioning
screens.subtitle: Keeping content fresh without overloading the origin

narration.text: Cache invalidation lets you remove objects from CloudFront caches before their TTL expires, forcing CloudFront to retrieve fresh content from your origin. Use targeted invalidations for specific paths, like an updated index. html or a patched image. While CloudFront supports invalidating specific patterns or even all objects with /*, frequent full invalidations are costly and increase origin load. A better pattern is asset versioning: update file names with a version or hash, for example main. css? v=2 or main. abcdef. css. Versioning avoids invalidation entirely for most updates and guarantees that new assets are fetched as new cache objects. Use invalidation sparingly for emergency or security-related changes that cannot wait for versioned deployment. Another operational practice is to track invalidation usage and watch origin metrics after an invalidation to ensure origin capacity handles the refill. A common misconception is that TTL tuning alone is sufficient; TTLs balance freshness and performance, but versioning plus selective invalidation provides controlled updates without global cache disruption. The takeaway: prefer versioned assets and reserve invalidations for exceptional circumstances while monitoring origin load during the refill period.

keyIdea.title: Invalidation strategy
keyIdea.text: Favor versioned assets to avoid frequent invalidations; use invalidation only for urgent updates and monitor origin performance afterward.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Invalidation & Versioning
Invalidate
Remove cached objects by path patterns. Use for urgent fixes, but be mindful of cost and origin load during cache refill.
Best practices
  • Invalidate specific paths rather than using /* when possible.
  • Monitor origin metrics after invalidation to verify capacity.
  • Automate invalidation as part of CI/CD for critical assets.
Versioning
Use unique file names or hashed filenames for new releases. This avoids invalidation and gives clients and caches a clear signal to fetch new assets.
Concrete example
Deploy main.abc123.js for a new release rather than invalidating main.js across all caches.

screens.title: Monitoring CloudFront Performance
screens.subtitle: Track metrics that guide tuning decisions

narration.text: Monitoring is the operational feedback loop that tells you when to change cache policies, enable Origin Shield, or adjust TTLs. Key CloudFront metrics to watch are cache hit ratio, origin latency, request count, and error rates. Cache hit ratio indicates how often objects are served from edge caches; a low ratio suggests excessive cache fragmentation or too many forwarded attributes. Origin latency and request count show origin load; spikes in origin requests after invalidation or a release can reveal capacity issues. Error rates can indicate misconfigurations or WAF rule overreach. Use logs and metrics together: access logs provide request-level detail for diagnosing why cache misses occur, while CloudWatch metrics give you aggregate signals for alerting. A practical pattern is to create alarms on origin request surge and low cache hit ratios, and to run a post-deploy check after invalidations or new releases. A common misconception is treating caching as set-and-forget. Instead, iterate: measure, adjust cache keys or TTLs, and validate the impact. The takeaway: let metrics drive configuration changes and use alerts to catch regressions quickly. Monitoring CloudFront Performance means make data-driven caching and protection decisions by tracking cache hit ratio, origin latency, and error signals.. In practical terms, track metrics that guide tuning decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Monitoring takeaway
keyIdea.text: Make data-driven caching and protection decisions by tracking cache hit ratio, origin latency, and error signals.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Monitoring
Cache Hit Ratio
Measure percent of requests served by cache. Low values indicate forwarding too many attributes or fragmentation.
Origin Latency & Requests
Track request count and latency to spot origin overloads, especially after invalidations or deployments.
Errors & WAF Logs
Monitor 4xx/5xx rates and WAF logs to tune rules and detect regressions introduced by protections or deployments.
Operational pattern
Create alarms on sudden origin request increases and low cache hit ratios, and run a short post-deploy validation to ensure metrics remain within expected thresholds.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: These key concepts summarize the chapter’s practical guidance. First, cache policies define what CloudFront forwards and the TTLs that drive cache behavior. Design cache keys by forwarding only essential attributes and use versioning to avoid frequent invalidations. Second, Origin Shield consolidates cache-miss traffic from multiple edge locations to the origin, reducing duplicate origin requests and improving origin resilience, particularly during global releases. Third, Lambda@Edge and AWS WAF let you apply security and request normalization at the edge. Use Lambda@Edge for lightweight, idempotent changes like adding headers or normalizing query strings, and use WAF to block common web exploits at the distribution layer. Together, these features lower origin load, improve performance, and protect application behavior. The final takeaway is to pair configuration with monitoring so you can measure impact and iterate safely.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Tune cache keys, protect origins with Origin Shield, and apply edge-level security while monitoring outcomes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Key Concepts
Cache Policy
Defines TTLs and which headers, query strings, and cookies determine cache keys.
Origin Shield
Centralized caching layer that reduces origin requests from multiple edge locations.
Edge Security
Use Lambda@Edge for lightweight modifications and WAF for application-layer protections at the distribution edge.
Summary

Combine careful cache key design, Origin Shield, and edge security controls, then validate and iterate with metrics to optimize performance and protect your origin.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Keep these three practical reminders at hand. First, always think about the cache key: forward the minimum attributes required for correctness and prefer versioned asset names over broad invalidations. Second, use Origin Shield to consolidate misses during high global demand or multi-CDN setups to protect origin capacity. Third, enforce consistent security at the edge: deploy Lambda@Edge for fast header additions or request normalization and integrate AWS WAF to block common web threats. Pair these configurations with monitoring so you can detect regressions and tune policies based on real traffic signals. These habits will help you reduce cost, improve user experience, and keep your origin resilient. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means design cache keys, protect origins with consolidation, and apply edge security while monitoring outcomes.. In practical terms, three practical reminders to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical reminders
keyIdea.text: Design cache keys, protect origins with consolidation, and apply edge security while monitoring outcomes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Key Concepts — Reference
Design cache keys
Minimize forwarded attributes; use versioning for updates.
Consolidate origin requests
Enable Origin Shield when global misses or multi-CDN patterns cause origin stress.
Apply edge security
Use Lambda@Edge for small modifications and WAF for application-layer protection at the edge.
Final thought
